steps.prompt: Which word starts a question about he, she or it?
steps.why: Does for he, she and it. Do for everyone else.
steps.html:
Do they like their jobs? — Yes, they do.

Does he play the piano? — Yes, he does.

Do you have a job? — No, I don't.

steps.title: Yes/no questions with do and does
steps.html:
PersonQuestionYesNo
I / you / we / theyDo you work here?Yes, I do.No, I don't.
he / she / itDoes he work here?Yes, he does.No, he doesn't.
with to beIs she a nurse?Yes, she is.No, she isn't.

After Do or Does the verb is the base form: Does he work…?, not Does he works…?

Short answers repeat do / does, not the main verb: Yes, he does.

to be does not use do: say Is she a nurse?, not Does she be a nurse?

steps.title: a / an with jobs
steps.html:
Before…UseExample
a consonant soundaShe's a nurse.
a vowel soundanHe's an engineer.
more than one personno a / anThey're nurses.

English always puts a or an before a job in the singular.

Learners often say She is nurse. It has to be a nurse.

steps.title: Which job makes people happy?
steps.html:
Every year researchers ask people the same four questions. Do you like your job? Does your work help other people? Do you work with a team? Does your job give you free time?

The answers are always a surprise. Pilots and dentists earn a lot of money, but they are not the happiest people. Office workers say they like their colleagues, but they hardly ever see the result of their work.

The winner is the hairdresser. A hairdresser usually works freelance, so she doesn't have a boss. She sees fifteen or twenty different people every day. And at the end, her customers look good and feel good. Does that make her happy? Yes, it does.
